opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a fair amount, because the headline time-horizon numbers can be a little misleading if you don't also look at cost. The basic approach is pretty simple: for each task, we have some estimate of how long it takes a skilled human professional to do it, and so you can translate that into a human labor cost, roughly hours times a reasonable hourly wage for someone with the relevant expertise. Then on the agent side, we look at the actual inference spend for the run, the tokens in and out, priced at whatever the API rates are.

And what we've generally found is that, for the tasks where agents succeed, they're usually much cheaper than the human baseline, often by a large factor, like a small fraction of what it would cost to pay a person. Even on the longer tasks, the ones that take humans multiple hours, the agent runs are typically in the range of a few dollars to maybe tens of dollars, versus hundreds of dollars of human time.

But there are a bunch of caveats I'd want to flag. One is that you have to account for failure. If the agent only succeeds some fraction of the time, the effective cost per successful completion goes up, and you also need some way to know whether it succeeded, which itself might require human review. Another is that the comparison depends a lot on how much scaffolding and how many tokens you let the agent use. You can sometimes buy higher success rates by spending more, with more attempts or more samples, and so there's really a curve rather than a single number. And then the human side is uncertain too: our baselines are people who might not have a ton of context on the specific codebase, so a real employee with context might be faster.

So I'd say the takeaway is that cost doesn't currently look like the binding constraint. When agents fail at longer tasks, it's mostly not because it got too expensive to keep going, it's that they get stuck, or go down the wrong path, or don't notice their own mistakes. But it's definitely something we want to keep tracking, because as people throw more inference compute at these problems, the cost picture could change.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a lot of time on with HCAST, and I think the honest answer is that the cost story is more complicated than people assume in either direction.

The naive version is: AI agents are cheap per token, humans are expensive per hour, so agents win. And on the short tasks, that's basically right. If you have a task that takes a human ten or fifteen minutes, the agent is often doing it for a couple dollars of inference, and even if it fails sometimes, you're still way ahead on cost.

But the thing we kept running into is that as the tasks get longer, two things happen at once. First, the agents just succeed less often. Our headline finding was that success rate degrades pretty sharply as a function of how long the task takes a human expert. So you're paying for a lot more failed attempts. Second, the cost per attempt also goes up, because the agent is taking more steps, re-reading context, running tools, sometimes going in circles. So you're multiplying a higher per-attempt cost by a lower success rate, and the expected cost per successful completion can balloon.

So the way we think about it is: what's the cost to actually get a correct output, not the cost per run. If you do that accounting on, say, tasks that take a human several hours, the agents often don't look that cheap anymore. In some cases you'd be better off just paying the person.

There's also the question of what you count. We measured human baseliner time fairly carefully, and those are skilled people being paid real wages. But there's a hidden cost on the AI side too, which is verification. If the agent hands you something and you can't tell whether it's right, someone has to check it, and on long, open-ended tasks that checking can take a substantial fraction of the time it would have taken to just do it. We tried to pick tasks with reasonably objective scoring to avoid that, but in the real world you don't get that luxury.

The last thing I'd say is that it's a moving target. The cost per token keeps dropping, and the success curves keep shifting right, so the crossover point where agents become cost-competitive on a given task length is moving too. I'd be a bit cautious about anyone giving you a fixed number. What I'd rather people take from our work is the shape of the relationship, and then plug in current prices and current capabilities for their own use case.

astra-6.text:
I think the relevant comparison is the cost of getting the task done successfully, rather than the cost of a single attempt. An agent might be much cheaper than a person per hour, but if it takes several attempts and someone has to spend a lot of time checking or repairing the result, that can erase the advantage.

For longer tasks, I’d want to know how reliably the agent makes progress, whether it can recover from mistakes, and how much human supervision it needs. There’s also a big difference between tasks where you can cheaply verify the final result and tasks where checking the work is almost as difficult as doing it.

So I wouldn’t infer cost competitiveness just from an agent succeeding on a long task. You need to measure the total cost across attempts, including failures and human involvement, and compare that with a human producing work of similar quality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much it costs to get a task completed successfully, rather than how much it costs to run an agent for a given amount of time. An agent might be much cheaper per hour than a human, but if it rarely finishes the task, or someone has to spend a lot of time checking and fixing its work, that can wipe out the advantage.

Longer tasks make this especially interesting because errors can compound. You want to measure the success rate, the cost of retries, and how much human supervision is required. And then compare that with what a human would actually take to do the same task, at a comparable level of quality.

So I’d be cautious about inferring cost competitiveness just from an agent succeeding once on a long task. That demonstrates a capability, but the economic question is whether it can do it reliably and cheaply across a representative set of tasks.
